utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, sir. Could you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth so help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petrovic. Thank you for coming back once again to the Tribunal. I have very few questions for you this morning. Let me just explain a bit, as I did when I met you on Tuesday. We had previously admitted your testimony from the Popovic case in this trial, but it was decided to -- that it would be best to bring you to answer some questions and help the Tribunal again. So just as in the Tolimir case, we are going to put in your testimony from the Popovic trial, and then you'll be asked some questions, primarily by Mr. Karadzic. I have -- do you recall that you testified in the Popovic case in 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes. General Borovcanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. And just as in the Tolimir case, I have a -- there is a couple questions about that testimony. Can you confirm that you reviewed it and that if you were asked the same questions today, you would give the same answers. Not word for word, but the same information. Basically that the transcript is correct.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes. The essence is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one correction that you made in Tolimir that I should put on the record here. At page 1880 there was a reference to a Colonel Brunel, B-r-u-n-e-l, and it should be Bunel, B-u-n-e-l; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [In English] Bunel, a French colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think, then, that concludes the attestation. The exhibits are all already admitted and I think we would keep the same numbers. I'll now read a brief summary. In July 1995, Mr. Petrovic-Pirocanac - Pirocanac is a nickname - was an independent journalist who was based in Belgrade, Serbia. On 13 and 14 July 1995, he accompanied RS MUP commander Ljubisa Borovcanin, who he was familiar with from before, to various places and filmed what he saw. Although he was not a professional cameraman, he brought a camera with him. On the 13th, they went to Potocari and also along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Mr. Petrovic filmed various now-famous scenes, men on the balcony of the white house in Potocari, Muslim men surrendering and being detained at Sandici meadow and bodies of men in front of the Kravica warehouse, amongst other footage shot that day. The next day, on the 14th of July, the witness filmed Tomo Kovac, Mr. Borovcanin, and Dragomir Vasic in Srebrenica and other places, and he interviewed various people including some Serb citizens who had returned to Srebrenica. Mr. Petrovic returned to Belgrade after shooting this film and very quickly edited the footage into a documentary which was then broadcast on Studio B in Belgrade. And Mr. Petrovic provided us with a copy of his "raw" footage, and some of the parts that we can see on the documentary are not on the raw footage. That concludes the summary. And I have no questions for you at this time, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Just for the record, we'll note that his transcript in Popovic et al. case is admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Petrovic shall I address you Mr. Petrovic or Pirocanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we know each other from previous -- [Interpretation] I'm sorry -- [In English] we know each other from previous case. Well, sir, you are commander here, so you do -- I am Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it is your choice, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Dr. Petrovic. As you noted, your evidence given in the case of Popovic et al. was admitted in lieu of your examination-in-chief, and then now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning, Excellency. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind both you and myself to be careful to make pauses because it seems that the interpreters are angry with me with forcing the pace.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, one sentence, if possible. Due to technical reasons, I would like to congratulate you on the 20th anniversary of Republika Srpska because without you, to a great extent, the Serbs wouldn't have had their state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And through you I would like to congratulate you on the international day of journalists, and that is today.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: And also it's a volunteers day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have another jubilee today. And with the Chamber's leave, I would like to ask you something else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, Dr. Petrovic, please put a pause before you start answering the question because bear in mind the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may suggest, you should probably look at the transcript and once you see that the interpretation is over, you can start your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You knew a lot about the political life in Bosnia and Herzegovina and how the conflict started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about any political issues, however, but what you as a journalist could find out at the time. Is it correct that with respect to the zone around Srebrenica you had some partially knowledge, and is it true that you found out that on the 29th of August, 1992, a captured Serbian soldier, captured in Podravanje, Muslim soldiers roasted him on a spit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes. Even in a book wrote [as interpreted] by a group of authors, I published this photograph. It's a man whose name I shall remember for as long as I live. He was born in 1958, and his photograph exists. He was roasted on a spit in 1992 on the 28th or 29th of August. What is interesting about this photograph is that it shows what kind of war that was. I have to admit to you now that I practically stole this photograph from Republika Srpska. I had some people who were able to extract that from the archives. I'll call them insiders because the principle of the JNA was still in force and the notion of brotherhood and unity was observed. Therefore, this photograph was considered a military secret. But I stole it and I published it this book, and that is why you know about it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that photograph part of the investigation material that was not conveyed to the public?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I didn't know the status of this photograph either at that time or today. I only found out its location. I managed to find people who had enough courage to get hold of this photograph for the sake of the truth. But it was totally out of the civilian reach, or the reach of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Quite early, you had an insight into the presence of foreign elements in our civil war, particularly those who came from Muslim countries, and I'm talking about the Mujahedin. Can you please tell the Chamber, how did you find out about the presence of Mujahedin? And then especially how did you learn about the presence of Osama bin Laden in Sarajevo and his encounters with Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: These are two things. Osama bin Laden didn't come immediately, as far as I know. Initially there were only small volunteer groups coming from various Islamic countries led by a few commanders who had experience from Afghanistan. They are called Afghan Saluni [phoen]. These are the best and most seasoned combatants. And that is what I heard about them, in addition to them being the fiercest and the most merciless fighters that Izetbegovic had at his disposal during the war. They appeared, according to my information, because, at the time, I worked for a small independent news agency called INA in Belgrade and had problems in dissemination this kind of news, because the official policy of Belgrade was still not to publish them in order not to disturb the western countries; because at the beginning of the war, NATO pact was providing considerable assistance to these combatants and to Mr. Izetbegovic's army in general, not so much by interfering but, rather, by allowing various things such as the use of the Tuzla airport for a major air transport of various ammunition and weapons that had been coming from Iran because they were allies with Iran at the time, and I also know that Turkish aircraft landed in Tuzla as well. So my news agency acquired information through, I have to say it here, some Israeli journalists, people from Israel who had close connections with their intelligence services, but also through a number of Serbian businessmen who, due to the nature of their work, knew more than ordinary businessmen. So we put together this puzzle of the presence of Islamic fighters there. I have to say that at the time I worked as a commentator on B92 radio station, and this information that I broadcast over the radio caused hilarious laughter among the majority of journalists, albeit not all of them, because nobody ever spoke in Europe before that time about the arrival of Mujahedin to Bosnia. I'm talking about the summer of 1992. I can speak more about this, but I'll make it short. Anyway bin Laden was detected. Beforehand I had some hints, but nothing tangible. I knew that bin Laden was organising his men to help his brethren in Bosnia, his brethren by religion. But I didn't have any solid evidence to that effect. I heard this information in a conversation that I had with a female journalist, a German journalist called Renate Flottau, and I mentioned her in my previous testimony. She was an official correspondent. She was a first-class or a first category journalist. Due to that, she had access to, most of all, the most important political figures in Yugoslavia, and, as far as I know, she even had contact with you and, of course, with President Alija Izetbegovic. So in that conversation, she confirmed to me something that she had already mentioned to one of our former correspondents from Germany - I cannot remember his name at the moment, although he is a prominent journalist, and I apologise for that - so I was the second person who heard this information and made it public; that is to say, I published it in a book about Al Qaeda which was printed in 2002. Nobody including from Bosnia ever refuted this, and Madam Flottau, before she entered the office of President Izetbegovic, told me that she had seen this man, this man two times. She described him as being rather talkative and wanted to attract attention. When I asked her why didn't she publish this because I would have been the happiest person in the world if I had an opportunity to interview him, she said something to the effect that nobody in her editorial office would take it seriously. They would think that that was a case of a lunatic talking about a variety of things. But being a professional journalist, I still find this to be quite odd because I would definitely mention this person in any of my writings. On the other hand, it shows that Madam Flottau was a highly respected journalist in Germany, and I'm sure that if she managed to interview bin Laden, that would stir great excitement all over the world. I'm sure of that. This little detail is important because of the location. She saw him later on conversing with Mr. Izetbegovic. I have to tell you that I don't know whether it was in 1993 or 1994. You'd have to ask Madam Flottau about this. And he wasn't as famous at the time as he was later, but everybody knew about Afghan fighters. And the proof that I was right when I spoke on B92 about this, because about a month later on that same radio, B92, the English press, I think that was "Sunday Times" published an interview on two or three pages with one of the first known leaders of Islamic volunteers. I still cannot remember his name, but I think that he stayed the longest in Bosnia after the war. Now, all of this was something that wasn't taken into consideration during the war, who was in league with whom. This fact relating to bin Laden didn't -- wasn't taken into consideration until the appearance of the information that was conveyed to me by Mrs. Plavsic and I wrote about that in "Nin" magazine; that is to say that the Serbs had bought this videotape from some Croats for about 20- or 30.000 German marks and that was the first time that everybody could see what they were -- what they were doing in Bosnia. However, this tape was only being played after 9/11 on numerous occasions, and it shows some of -- shots from the NATO offensive with El Mujahid Brigade attacking fortified Serbian positions on Mount Ozren. I also find it resentful that Republika Srpska failed to make use of it because, on that occasion, depleted uranium bombs were used, because that was the only way that they could have done anything against the Serbs and I think that this lasted for ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to -- to leave this subject. We don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Well, this refers to bin Laden.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if we have time, I would be glad to hear what Dr. Petrovic has to say about everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind your motion, Mr. Karadzic. You asked for this witness to be called for certain purpose. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you this, Dr. Petrovic: Is it correct that the Bosnian war was not a first war for you. You had some previous experience. And can you tell us which wars you had an opportunity to see and if you can draw any parallels between them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, from 1979, which is 13 years before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was a reporter from Nicaragua with a colleague of mine. He was the only freelance journalist from that part of the Europe. Of course, there were journalists from the "Politika" daily, Tanjug, et cetera. That was my first war experience. I witnessed some very turbulent events, such those in Poland, but that was not war. Then in 1985, I was in Lebanon. And I was stuck there, if I may say so, for many days, because after ten days upon my arrival, I and my cameraman were arrested and we were kept somewhere in the mountains of Lebanon. After that, I went to Israel because Israel has been in a state of war for decades and I covered various events from Israel, both political ones and conflicts. I also participated in our civil war as a reporter. In a nutshell, I can say that I was present at major points of conflicts such as Vukovar, Stolice at Mount Majevica near -- then in Sarajevo, Dobrovoljacka street, and the environs of Srebrenica. That would be in a nutshell. As for the similarities, after I left Lebanon in 1985, I wrote about my impressions, and in a way, I predicted what was going to happen in Yugoslavia because there was a multi-ethnic situation in Lebanon as well and then the ensuing war, although, let me remind you, that you never declared a state of war in the whole of territory, which in my eyes was a mistake. Wars were often waged according to the Lebanese model. Village A against village B, then village B against village C, and that was endless fighting in which neighbours were killing each other. And for me, that was a striking similarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to July 1995, but if time remains today, I'd like you to tell us a bit about the Dobrovoljacka street incident. Were you with JNA column that was pulling out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. And you can still find the issue of the "Duga" bi- weekly magazine. I published an article there called: "The war in Sarajevo," with a special chapter called: "The convoy," where I described very much in detail my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've made attempts to go to Srebrenica as a journalist in July 1995. Could you tell us very briefly about all the things you had to go through, all the hoops you had to jump through to get there during the war.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls mentioned it. It's already in my evidence from before, but I can repeat briefly. I'm already tired of repeating these things. Any journalists wants to go where the action is, and Srebrenica had been attracting the attention of the international public for years by then. Some people had tried to get into Srebrenica with the Americans when the food was being brought to people in the town. I apologise. On the 11th, I found from the news, like all the other journalists, that Serb had entered Srebrenica. I got in touch with Studio B immediately because I worked as a war reporter throughout the war working with the French television ITN, and I agreed with the editor-in-chief, or, rather, the programming director of Studio B, Mr. Oganovic, but unfortunately did not manage to get a camera from them because it was a rather poor television station that did not have enough equipment, cameras or editing equipment. So, in the end, I took with me an 8-millimetre video camera, the kind tourists have, plus I'm not a professional cameraman and I know nothing about the filming, the quality of the image or anything. It was a disaster that it was the only thing I could do because I could not bring a cameraman. And then I went to the border, to the bridge leading to Bratunac on the Drina river, and I was turned back from there. That was on the 12th. I was turned back because they said the operation was ongoing. It was a war zone. Nobody, including journalists, could get access until the operation is over. And the operations were planned to last for another two weeks and they did. So I went back to Belgrade to the police brigade, and I found Colonel Borovcanin and told him that, among other things, I placed a call to the VRS, a man of whom I have a bad memory, Colonel Milutinovic, who told me, tongue in cheek, Pirocanac, it is not against you personally but we'll arrest anyone who shows up there while the operation is underway. So I asked Borovcanin, whom I knew from before, I had been with him at Mount Majevica and Semizovac, and they knew my professional record. I was a journalist of some renown, if I may say so, and he agreed to take me on the 13th. Mr. Nicholls knows that there was a problem with dates. Sometimes the date indication on the film would disappear when I pressed the wrong button, and it -- but the film shows that I was at the Dutch compound on the 13th. Those are the first images. I must say, Mr. Borovcanin agreed immediately. He didn't put any conditions. He didn't impose any restrictions. He just said, You know your job. You can film anything. And that's exactly what happened. And it was thanks to this honest man, Mr. Borovcanin. Thanks to him the Court has these very valuable images. And I'm not sorry, although I went through hell because of this film. Many images on it have been deleted. Mr. Nicholls mentioned it. Perhaps at one point, this Court received my original film of 28 minutes with a logo of the Studio B and then it disappeared. How could it have disappeared from the locked cupboard of the programming director? That's the only tape that ever disappeared from the Studio B. I'm inclined to think that somebody stole it and sold it, or perhaps the programming director himself who had family connections with the military somehow made it available to the military intelligence. But I dubbed the film on a VHS tape and sent it to some family in Canada, and that saved me because that original film contains all the so-called vanished images from my raw material, and that raw material is also historic, a precedent, because this tape made the rounds among the journalists and the public. I made it available to everyone. But I will perhaps even sue the SENSE agency that works here in the building. They have been using it for years and making money on it. It's time, perhaps, for me to get finally rich, and I believe this Court should be eternally grateful to Mr. Borovcanin that he let me go there without any censorship; because, if they had plans to commit any killings, they would have killed me immediately. I have been saying this for years. They would have liquidated me if they had any criminal plans at the time; or, why would they have engaged somebody from the outside when they could have done the filming themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's stay a bit with the Colonel Milutinovic. Is that the Colonel Milutinovic who was chief of the army press centre and who made his own films in Srebrenica? And did you understand that perhaps he was protecting his monopoly by refusing you access?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: It turned out that among the NGOs that were helping when the Muslims were leaving for Tuzla, and very soon, 28.000 of them left immediately. There was a journalist, Rohl Havim [phoen]. He simply infiltrated himself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to speak more slowly so that everything is recorded.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Among those people, there were at least several western journalists. I was not the only one there. There were several reporters from Serbia who got in. But I was perhaps more of a celebrity than most of them, and perhaps they didn't want me to come more than anyone else. One of these agencies characterised my reporting as hearsay, but they can't understand that it's very difficult to know everything. I know that a lot of material turned up in various trials here gathered by members of the VRS. And that's natural because there was a service responsible for such things in the VRS. How was this filmed during the war? How did it find its way to various lawyers in this Tribunal? We don't know. But he belonged to Mladic's staff, and he had a free hand in many ways. He was a very influential man. Based on the fact that he had influence, you can draw a lot of conclusions but I didn't do that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there also a Swedish reporter in Srebrenica at the time? I don't know his name, but I see that you mentioned a Swedish reporter in the Tolimir case, page 14485. So it was possible to get there in various ways?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That's true. I believe there were no less than ten reporters there. I never managed to find out, and due to the trauma I experienced over the Srebrenica case, I didn't properly try. I never managed to write a book about Srebrenica which is a shame. It would have been better than most that had been published. But I heard from various colleagues in Belgrade there had been a Swedish journalist there. I don't remember the name I was told. But if a team were to work on it, they could look through all that was published in the Swedish press at the time, including interviews with Bosnian people who made their way to Sweden, who were sharing their fresh impressions. It was authentic reporting. People had -- were still in shock from all the fighting that was still ongoing, the heat, the travel. You could certainly find his name there. Why did I mention him? In all these texts that I published, I made a claim, making a mistake concerning time. I mentioned 24th of July. I described the operation that was never covered in our media; namely, that the Muslims who had descended from Srebrenica regrouped in that area in a -- into a wedge one night. I said 21st, 22nd, 24th, but it must have been the 13th or the 14th. And there was a great danger that they could start breaking through, not simply straight to Tuzla but turn right and reach Zvornik, which was a town of strategic importance on the border with Serbia on the Drina river and that would have been a turn-around in the war. That was cause for great fear among the Serbs who were always short of people, and I was told that several thousand of Muslims died then. And your own police brigade suffered the greatest losses that night, lots of dead and wounded. Somebody told me there were 88 dead, and somebody told me those were the highest losses of a professional unit like that through the whole war and lots of others had told me that they barely survived it - that's why I remember it - and the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clear up a few things, and I hope you will be able to answer very briefly, perhaps with a yes or no. Is it true that you never felt that the civilian authorities, and Borovcanin and his unit were part of civilian authorities, had any reservations or were trying to prevent your presence in that zone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Coming back to what the army said that I shouldn't go there and that if I was found there I would be arrested and my agreement with Borovcanin that I would be able to film that on the sole condition that I should stick to him, not because he wanted to check what I was filming, but in order not to be arrested by the army. I must say that that's what the army told everyone. Nobody ever asked me any questions or tried to stop me from filming, as long as I was near Borovcanin. But it's true that I would have been arrested by the army as soon as I arrived, probably at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a few weeks later, in Zepa, there were journalists present, and I personally enabled Peter Arnett from the American TV station, ABC, I think, and do you know that the agency Crna was planning to send foreign journalists into all these areas as soon as the fighting stopped; in other words, did the authorities or the police want journalists there, actually, to avoid mystification?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I did not go back to that area, but all of us journalists in Belgrade knew that many foreign correspondents had gone to Zepa. We knew these people. They were based in Belgrade. And nobody was hiding anything. And it would have been very stage for journalists to have been allowed to go there and film while there was a genocidal plan in the making. I never had any indication of that from all the talk I had with these people, with these foreign journalists with whom we shared a press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said earlier today and in your earlier testimony, but please confirm once again, Colonel Borovcanin did not impose on you any restrictions, in terms of features you were allowed to film, or your choice of theme and what you could film. Is it true that you had complete freedom in that respect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. It was a relationship of mutual respect and openness based on two prior occasions when we had gotten to know each other at Majevica which was a very important communications hub and there was a lot of fighting around it. Serbs were surrounded, encircled, near the repeater. The photographer from our crew didn't dare to go there, but I went, and I saw those Afghan fighters shouting, Takbir, takbir. It was a frightening sight. There was a very small unit there, but they must have told Borovcanin later about my demeanour, and I didn't make any problems for them in the field. I wrote very honestly about everything, and that was guarantee enough for him. He did not -- did he not worry about me at all, except -- except for not wanting me to get arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I hadn't been here in a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few things which were the reason why I called you here. Did you meet the journalist called Robert Block?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: My first association concerning him is something that is probably improper to utter here. But, briefly, I would say that he was a dishonourable person and a dishonourable reporter. I saw him for maybe a minute, not longer, in Bratunac. But I think it is very important, if you allow me to continue. In a situation when Milutinovic told me that he was going to arrest me, including all the other journalists, because Milutinovic had nothing personal against me. That was the position of the command. I was completely stunned in that situation because I saw this man in Bratunac, Bratislav Grubacic, who used to work for the Tanjug press centre. I asked Bratislav, How come that you are here? And he answered by saying something which is more than ridiculous, and he knows it was a ridiculous answer, and he said, Well, we were a little bit travelling around Bosnia and we dropped by to see what was going on here. In my opinion, this is a imbicile sentence. I apologise for using this term. And I don't remember us discussing anything else apart from this. Maybe we exchanged a sentence or two more and then they left. They were foreigners but they were never arrested by army. Also important is that in an article by Michael Dobbs, a respectable journalist, published in the foreign policy journals where he analyses the case of Kravica, and I saw that he said in this article that Block had been in Studio B after his arrival, and that he was reviewing my pre-edited material, which is something unheard of. And everything that Block wrote about, starting from the 15th or 16th of July, were mainly lies, because he was the one who set rolling this story about genocide in Srebrenica. I think he was one of the key people entrusted with this task. I cannot give you an exact quote, but I remember him mentioning one thousand people killed in a school in Bratunac which is total rubbish. And later on it turned out to be real rubbish. So that's the kind of journalist that he was. So I despise him. I especially resent his statement that he had visited me in my home. The then-girlfriend of Bratislav Grubacic was there. She was a secretary at the Dutch embassy in Belgrade, and she is today the wife of the ambassador to Zagreb. He was a member of the delegation of the Dutch Royal Institute but she misrepresented her position. That is the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So his claim that he visited you and that you gave him the tape and that you discussed this topic at all is untrue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: It is absolutely untrue and dishonourable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: His claim that you gave him the tape. What does that refer to? Can I have a cite, in the last question? I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Block saying that Mr. Petrovic-Pirocanac gave him a tape. I may be wrong, but I'd like a cite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Block say that Mr. Petrovic gave the tape to him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I think I am mixing up Blasik and Block.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Block stated here that he had been at his home, that he discussed the situation, that he heard something from Mr. Pirocanac. And I'm going to ask Mr. Pirocanac whether that was correct or not, and I apologise to Mr. Nicholls for being inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can freely speak in Serbian for the sake of our public.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is my third testimony in The Hague, and I never told untruth in any of my answers. It is utterly senseless to speak something like that. I would like to state clearly that this man is a liar. He's not telling the truth. The only explanation I can think of is that he is re-telling the story about the journalist whose wife was Dutch and then on the Internet he said that I abruptly ended this conversation. This Dutch journalist is using this raw material also and he is trying to find out what many people in Belgrade found out and claim that I erased some of my footage. But he must know that there is an original programme, and this Court knows that as well because it contains all these missing fragments and probably Block is confusing this situation. It is this Dutch journalist with a local cameraman, and this can be testified to by my family and by this cameraman. But Block never visited me at my home. We just greeted each other in Bratunac, and that was the only time we met, and I really wouldn't wish to have him as a friend. He is a liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, let us establish the following: So what was broadcast in the programme and what this Court has in its possession contains each and every scene and each and every frame, including everything that is missing from the raw material?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. That's the white house and the two or three seconds before Kravica, which was shot from the moving car. But there's another footage, ten or 15 seconds, about Sandici. There is no dispute about that. And this footage of Kravica and Bela Kuca [phoen] was invaluable for this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Block said here that you had told him that you had enormous problems that even I was angry because you had gone to Srebrenica to shoot your film; is that correct? Did you have any impression that either I personally or our entire leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik, held it against you? Did you have any problems with us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just let -- let it go for the moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things. I remember that Studio B was asked by the leadership of Republika Srpska to have the programme shown to them. Someone sent it by bus. I mean, bus was the only way of communicating. It's not really that many people travelled to Bosnia then. So they did not have -- I mean, there were no negative reactions. Absolutely none. No one from the leadership of Republika Srpska reacted in a negative way. I don't know whether you viewed it then. I don't think so. But the other leaders did view it, all the top leaders. Secondly, I interviewed you three times during the war. Our last encounter was in your house in December 1994. In 1995, I didn't see you as all, and, as far as I can remember, I didn't even speak to you. I don't know what the date was when the UNPROFOR soldiers were taken prisoner. I intervened for a Spanish diplomat, but I did not have any contact with you. And everybody would have told me had you minded anything and if you were angry in any way. So that's an absolute lie. I don't know. Nowadays, good journalists can be great liars, although that is pointless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, I'll hear you now, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I withdraw it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about me being angry at Milutinovic? And that what I was angry about was because he was doing Mladic a disservice and portraying this as his victory, neglecting Krstic, and I even heard rumours to the effect that he had sold some footage. Did you hear any of that, that perhaps I was angry at him? I spoke about that at an assembly meeting but not because of the actual recording but because of this self-promotion and lack of impartial reporting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really cannot help you with that, as far as the selling of the cassette is concerned. I don't know what people were saying about me as well, that I had sold my things to God knows who. But among the journalists who were following the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was often mentioned, that people from the military were actually doing the recording but I don't have any proof of that. However, I have to say that you were popular among journalists. You were considered to be an open man, and I remember that you criticised the army through that press service of theirs because of the way in which they acted. Often, they were actually doing Mladic himself a disservice. Today I think that that was no accident, that all these disservices were done, and that there were people who had to do things like that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about these restrictions, as far as journalists were concerned, close to the front line. In these other wars, did you also notice that commanders do not want journalists close to the front line, or was that only the case in our war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this behaviour changed during these wars and as time went by; for example, in Lebanon when I first reported, the Israelis wanted you to sign a piece of paper first, taking upon yourself the risk that you did run of being killed at the front line. As far as I can remember, your people did not ask for that, but journalists were everywhere. I know what your position was towards Martin Bell and Christiane Amanpour. Many times, they managed to do things that Serb journalists could not do. Since this is a war where there was no uniform position -- I mean, having a state of war declared throughout the territory, then there were different regional improvisations on the ground. Commanders, officers, the civilian authorities during this state of war, and so on and so forth. So I did not notice any kind of uniform behaviour, except for the fact that you always asked to have everything given to journalists. And that's how I managed to work, too. And it wasn't only me. It was French TV, for instance, TF1. You allowed them to do a great many things. I don't know whether this is a satisfactory answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I was interested in, whether it was only we. I know that soldiers were suspicious, and I believe that that's the way in any army. I just want to know whether that was a uniform sort of thing. I wanted to remind you of something that you said in your interview with the OTP on the 28th of February, 2006.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please call up 1D5633. And then the page is 112. The English version. I think it's all in English. I don't even know whether we do have a Serbian version. Yes, it seems that we have the Serbian version too. I don't know whether it's page 112 in Serbian as well. In English, I do know it's page 112, line 17. It starts with line 17 on page 112 in English. So can we take a look at that. There's a reference to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can help Mr. Karadzic, I think it may be page 115 in the English, speaking of e-court pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] [As read] "I just can suppose that in this field of Milosevic was still in power. Somebody came and it was astonishing, but what is important also that the leadership of Bosnia, Bosnian Serbs, Krajisnik, and others asked Studio B and me to send them a copy, the same as the next day it was aired. And I remember -- and I know the guy, his name is Zoran - he is now on "Politika" - he could confirm that we sent by bus copy to them, to Pale. They were still together. I don't know if Karadzic saw it but most of them saw it, and there they -- if you ask Krajisnik now if he remembers that, that it was very well done." [Interpretation] So did you get any feedback from the authorities of Republika Srpska to the effect that your work had been done properly and that there were no objections raised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. For example, that's a detail that I cannot recall with precision after so many years. But I know that, number one, there was no public reaction; and, secondly, some journalists from Pale. Now was it someone from television or these cameramen who work for foreign crews - there were some cameramen who worked for AP Television and I should also sue them on account of this footage - I don't know who it was who said that to me, but they said that people were satisfied. Just a small correction here. I guess it's my fault when I talked to Mr. Nicholls in Belgrade about this. I see this document here. I think that I made a mistake there. I think that they had seen the programme. Someone from Belgrade had told them about the programme and then the next day, or, rather, the next evening, the cassette was sent to Pale by bus. Zoran was a man who worked on satellite TV. He was in "Politika" then. I don't think he works in "Politika" now. But he is the man who knows about the cassette that went to Pale. There were no negative reactions, absolutely, and the journalist [Realtime transcript read in error "adjournment"] said that they were satisfied. That's what they told me. Perhaps you remember these two journalists from TV AP, dark with a moustache. One of them worked on TV Sarajevo before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Radoje something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Something like that that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 14 in the transcript, it should say "journalist", but over here it says ... it says "adjournment." That is what was typed, "adjournment." It shouldn't be "adjournment." It should be "journalist." So it was journalists who said this to you; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, can pages 15 and 16 from the interview be admitted. I mean 115 and 116, from the OTP interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a bit of patience, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask you a few more things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you strolled through Srebrenica. Did you see any buildings that had just been hit or that had just been burned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, like in my previous statements, I can only repeat what I stated. I have some war experience. I did not see anything like that. I was mainly in the main street, and perhaps I went up to some buildings in the centre, 10 or 15 metres, but these were not fresh traces. There was no smoke rising from buildings that had been set on fire. I just saw some smoke from the destroyed timber factory above Sarajevo. I can't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Above Srebrenica, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of that factory. But we could see signs of the initial fighting between the Serbs and Muslim when the Muslims were surrounded, but that was one or two years old. But there were absolutely no fresh traces. I believe that everybody had left, that everybody went to Bratunac down that road and that that was the best that could be done. I even recorded something in the centre, some corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you miss anything? Did you omit to record anything important?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not spend the entire day there. My time was limited because of the minister's visit, so I just managed to stroll a bit. Was it half an hour, an hour. I saw these three corpses, some dogs. You can see that on my footage. As an experienced person, I tried to see whether there were any traces, whether there were any dead, et cetera. Only later on I heard that an elderly lady - I remember her last name was the same as mine, Petrovic. She was 82 or 83. I have a photograph at home - she had had her throat slit when they were fleeing to Bratunac, but did I not see any of that. The mosque was still there. The church was still there. The department store was damaged. I entered an apartment. In the raw material you can even see what is there in that apartment. People left in a hurry. And I recorded the people who were coming back, the Serbs who had fled when the war started. That's how the war in Srebrenica started, this member of parliament who was ambushed. So people were coming back and they were carrying cooking oil and other things coming from US Aid, and I know they were walking from Bratunac, and I interviewed some of them in their houses, for instance. That's like what I saw in the Beqaa valley, Jerusalem Forever, et cetera. There were things like that in Srebrenica, but apart from these two or three dead bodies, I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The white house you recorded that and we have that footage. What was your assessment? How many people were there on the terrace, and did you receive any information to the effect that these persons were crime suspects?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That is the footage that was held against me for years. People were saying that I had erased it. That's in the original programme. You saw it just as the Prosecution did and just as the Court did. Let me repeat this once again. I'm recording this, these scenes in this heat, and may I say again that I was terribly shocked by the number of people there. And then these young children, women, elderly men, they're helping them board buses, trucks, and I am recording heaps of old clothing that no one would really want to wear. I'm not a cameraman, and cameraman have a rule, whether they're going to move left or right or whether they're just going to keep the camera still. So I moved to the right and I see this house, and I did not pay any attention to it when I was in the compound. I was interested in people, not the house. And then what I saw in the camera, through the camera, was the terrace combined with wood. It's half of the terrace that I have in my house. Half of my terrace would be, say, ten people. I mean, you can see through it. Can you see it in the camera. They're sitting. As far as I can remember, none of them were standing. So about ten people. I didn't know then but I asked later who those people were. And basically what I heard was that they were being investigated for crimes. I did not pay attention to that because I recorded a lot of other footage as you could see in my report. And that was also filmed. I didn't have a plan then. I didn't really think about it. I was just looking at images. I just wanted to have images for my viewers. That's what you do on TV. You want to have images that are telling. My recording was very poor, but many proved to be invaluable for the Court, and for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the film or -- and was it the case in reality that there was no tension, no fear, no coercion, that the situation was quite relaxed, that everybody was moving around freely and looking for something that they wanted to get their hands on? In other words, did you record any fear of Dutch soldiers among the civilians or any other people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, later on, when the debate started in the Netherlands about whether they had protected those people and should they have offered assistance to the Serbs, I had an opportunity to see those people in various situations. The first one was a discussion between an UNPROFOR officer from Africa and the Serb side about water supply, then I saw a black Dutch soldier who was pushing a wheelchair with an old man, then I saw another one drinking milk straight from the bottle. I even saw some of them who were armed and who were in the background footage of that compound. So some of them kept their weapons. I also filmed the officer whom I asked at the very outset what was going on here, but he told me, You know what's going on. And I say, No, I don't know. I've just come from Belgrade. He was a bit nervous, but I didn't notice, I don't care if it came from the Serbs, but I didn't hear anyone saying anything bad about those people. I also didn't see any triumphalism among the Serbs for entering Srebrenica. I didn't see anyone laughing. The people were simply exhausted, the soldiers, but nobody said anything abusive or bad. So you can partly detect this impression in my footage, which is a good testimony to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, no objection. Just to be clear, I assume Mr. Karadzic was talking about the 13th in his question, because, of course, Mr. Petrovic filmed on 13th and 14th. And in his question, at line 23/24, Mr. Karadzic sort of built in the 14th as well when he said that: "... everyone was moving around freely and looking for something that they wanted to get their hands on." Mr. Petrovic, in his description of the 14th and in his video of the 14th, shows Serb civilians returning once the town has been emptied looking for things to get their hands, going back to houses, taking different items. So, just for clarity, I'm trying to see which days we're talking about and which people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, could you be more specific in putting the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember mentioning the 14th at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I -- can I help?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can clarify it for us, what was the date on which he filmed this footage in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nicholls is right. You can see from the footage that the date is there. I was on the 13th in the compound filming the people who were preparing to leave Srebrenica, both those originally from Srebrenica and the refugees. On the 13th, I was filming them en route to Tuzla. And then on the 14th, along with Borovcanin, who was escorting the minister of police, I was in Srebrenica. At that time, the journalists were still banned from coming in, but since I was with Borovcanin I could enter. So Srebrenica itself is the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's -- it's my mistake because I consider Potocari to be also part of Srebrenica, and the Srebrenica itself was filmed on the 14th. Thank you. Now as for the things that you saw on the 13th, were you referring only to what was happening outside the white house, or are you referring to everything that was happening in different places with relation to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was speaking about these bundles.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: There were things carried by people in their hands. Those were small bundles, and they were preparing to board the buses. But I saw this huge pile, I think it was 6 or 7 metres high, a pile of totally worthless clothing. Not even the vagabonds in Paris would be willing to wear that. I don't know what the reason was. Maybe there was some contagious disease there. But, anyway, those were extremely poor clothing. That's what I saw, and I don't know why it was piled up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the previous question, which Mr. Nicholls referred to, you asked as follows: "Was it the case in reality that there was no tension, no fear, no coercion, that the situation was quite relaxed, that everybody was moving around freely and looking for something that they wanted to get their hands on? In other words, did you record any fear of Dutch soldiers among the civilians or any other people?" Were you asking the situation on the 13th in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm talking about what we saw in the film. There were no people in Srebrenica on the 14th. They were in Potocari, civilians and the soldiers alike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did it include the people in the white house as well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as the white house is concerned, I only wanted to hear from him whether he was able to estimate how many people were there and what they were doing on this balcony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us continue, unless Mr. Petrovic has anything to add to what he already said. Thank you. Given the time, shall we take a break now? We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, you mentioned a moment ago that there were a lot of old things heaped somewhere. I'll try to ask my questions so you can answer them with a yes or no. Was there a real danger of contagion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe so, if you look at the footage and see those old things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly call P194.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to clarify, from that point of view, the report you made.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both the Serbian and the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes it was published by Milomir Maric in a magazine called "Interview," published by the Politika publishing house, but it has not existed since the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you authored it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure of my knowledge of English, but this heading in English seems to suggest that it refers to a cover-up of the situation. Literally it says, "Whitewashing and begun," and I understand it As the beginning of disinfection of the town and clearing up; whereas in English it sounds like some sort of cover-up. How would you like this heading that you put to be translated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, it's obvious that the English term is wrong, "whitewashing." I meant repainting houses. Specifically painting inside the house, and it's important to read the text carefully because then you will see that. There is a passage where I depict one dimension of it in a very documentary way, and it was even misunderstood in Belgrade at a public debate where you were not invited, of course. There was a civilizational component to this conflict that is poorly perceived in the world very often. Let's put it this way: The Christian population uses more pork, whereas the Muslim population tends to use more lamb. And everybody from our part of the world can tell you that Christians frequently find the smell of lamb unpleasant emanating from the walls and inside the house, and Muslims object to the smell of pork. It's a fact. I went to Srebrenica often and I met a lot of people who went back there and they have to do house painting every few years. It's absolutely not about whitewashing. I would say interior house repainting. That was the meaning I meant when I was writing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm going to get additional time so I have to hurry up, and I'd like to cover the main things. You were at Sandici, around what time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: It was sometime in the afternoon, 3.00, 4.00 p.m., as soon as I finished filming inside the compound in Potocari, then we went to Bratunac and went further along that road. It must have been around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. I think you can see it on the footage when it shows the Serbs shooting from the road towards the mountains.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Nicholls on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. I just notice for the record that the witness is referring to some papers in front of him that appear to be highlighted when answering the questions. I hadn't noticed that before. I don't know what they are. He did tell me that when he met with Mr. Karadzic, that Mr. Karadzic gave him some papers. So I just, for the record, wonder what he is referring to. He looked down and to check his memory, I suppose, about what time he was in Sandici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic, if could you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. This is a summary of my case which contains concern passages where Mr. Karadzic marked or indicated the areas of questioning he would conduct today. I did not have time to consult it regularly, but what we are discussing now does not strictly adhere to what is indicated in my text. I have the English version here, and it is marked which parts of the text Mr. President Karadzic would like to highlight in our discussion today. But if it's a problem I can do without it. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We call it chronology. Those are quotations from everything that the witness has ever said anywhere. Citations. We are not trying to set any ambushes, and it's not unlike what the Prosecution does when they show him 92 ter documents and ask him what stands behind it, and there are references indicated below as to where -- where he said what and at what time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can provide it to anyone of the parties for inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you like to take a look?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wouldn't mind taking a look. I was just going to ask what it is, whether it's a prior transcript or something created by the Defence or what -- I just don't know what it is. And I would remark that it is not like our practice of 92 ter witnesses to -- I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If the usher would help the witness to hand over the document briefly to Mr. Nicholls. And, in the meantime, your evidence would have more probative value if you can testify not relying on that document you prepared. However, if necessary, you can tell us, and take a look at what you prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have here a few of my own articles that I brought. I have not re-reviewed them. I can provide them as well. I don't need them for these proceedings, but I took them just in case. I don't need them for my testimony here. I can hand this over too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tendered some of those articles. Could we now see 1D5634. It's one of those texts, and perhaps it is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's your glossary of war-time Sarajevo published in "Nin" magazine or perhaps "Duga" magazine. No, it's "Duga." It's rather a bad copy, but we have a translation. This relates mainly to the Dobrovoljacka street, your description of the incident at Dobrovoljacka street where the military column, which you accompanied as a journalist, was attacked and butchered.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is part of my article published in the "Duga" magazine in May 1992 after this incident which happened on the 3rd of May, and it's part of a very long glossary. I believe it's 20 type written pages relating this incident involving the military column that I accompanied with the TF 1 French television crew, and we were trying to prepare that report by that evening, so we got out at 1805 hours and that saves us, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here, "Dozens of armed civilians, Green Berets." To the best of your knowledge, was the difference between civilians and soldiers during our war not so much in clothing as in whether they were carrying weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With this French crew, I was in Sarajevo, both in end February and early March and in end April/early May. I was able to observe the rising of this war-time psychosis and the conversion of civilians into armed citizens. A funny, rather hilarious term was in use in Sarajevo at the time, spontaneously organised citizens, quote/unquote, and I noticed that in the incident with the convoy on the 3rd of May, 1992, because when they surrounded the car we were in, driven by the French reporter, Louis Beroux [phoen], they had all sorts of weapons, including, state-of-the-art weapons, from pistols and small arms, to Kalashnikovs and hand-made bombs and grenades. And it was all very tense and very dangerous because this was not a regular military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If a person like that got killed, and somebody else took their weapon, then a casual observer would say, seeing the body, that it was a civilian, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. That would be the first thing you would think in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this. We have translation for only two or three of these passages, no more than one page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object until -- to it being other than marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have to admit this in order to understand some meaning of the phrases. But given the position of the Prosecution, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2252, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the Sandici meadow. In your estimate, how many prisoners did you see at Sandici? How many did your camera record?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are many ways to count people in situations involving crowds, such as football matches, et cetera, or riots. At the time I was there, I thought there was enough to fill one bus, around 100 people. That's what I would say, and I believe that's what I said in my previous statements and evidence. It's hard to say, but that's the number that stuck in my head.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 03177 -- or, rather, 117. 65 ter 03117.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, is this a smaller or a larger part of what the camera filmed, or are they all of them? All of the people who were at Sandici around 2.00?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: This is a still from my video report. From this angle, you can't see all of them, but there were not many more. Perhaps double of what you can see in the picture, enough to fill a bus. Because this was filmed from lower ground, and some could not be seen in the view-finder, there were a few more than you can see here, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you went on towards Konjevic Polje. You stayed there a while. And during that time, Colonel Borovcanin found out about the incident at Kravica; correct? And then you went back.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Something like that. That's in the same area where these people were, the incident in which one fighter was wounded. Borovcanin found out almost immediately, and then we went back to the hospital for him - for Borovcanin - to see what happened to the soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, do we need to tender this still?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If necessary, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2253, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you just have passed the time allotted to you. How much time would you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in line with my submission, I can finish within ten or 15 minutes, but I believe it would be useful for the Trial Chamber if this witness were to tell us a great many things that he knows. But if we are going to stick to what the motion says, then I'll finish within 15 minutes. May I just say something, Excellencies? You see, how 92 bis is deficient. You see how a live person can turn his own statements into a live statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue. And conclude in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has a number been assigned to this image? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you returned. And you're sure that neither you nor Borovcanin at the time of the incident in Kravica, you were not near Kravica. You were even further away from Sandici towards Konjevic Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you mean the incident of the wounding of the Serb soldier by the Muslim soldier who had surrendered, we have not seen that at all. That is my recollection. We hadn't seen what happened at all. We just remember that somebody called Borovcanin and that we immediately set out to the hospital in Bratunac so that he could see that soldier. Obviously he cared about that soldier a great deal. It's probably one of his men from his unit, probably with a great deal of experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then from the car, the camera filmed the warehouse with a certain number of bodies. Do you remember whether the door, whether the door was closed where the bodies had been piled up? I think you testified along those lines. I think you said something like the door was closed, or something like that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if my memory serves me well, I think that I confirmed that during my previous testimonies. You should just know what the situation is when you're filming. I mean, I just held the camera in my hands then as the car was passing. It was one, two, three, probably not more than that. It was only later that I saw that there was a soldier that had been filmed and I saw that the door had been closed, and I was scandalised. Why did many witnesses base their testimony about the number of dead on the basis of an open door? Thank you for putting this question. I have a great deal of difficulty with this, because of the manipulation involved. If we recall the Borovcanin trial in 2007, we will see that until this day date, 2012, the only evidence that the world has, in spite of all the satellite imagery of this world, is only my footage of these few seconds where you can see about 15 or 20 dead persons - that's my estimate - is regards what happened in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't mean to object, but the question was: Was the door opened or closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Petrovic, if you try to answer the question. Mr. Karadzic will ask further questions, if necessary. But did you say your video is the only evidence about what happened in Kravica? I have to tell you that you we have some survivors and other witnesses. Yes, please continue. So did you answer the question, whether door was opened or closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, apologise, Your Excellency. I just wanted to be of assistance. The door was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that this is the only evidence, did you mean that it was the only video material?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As far as I know, it's that footage of mine and American satellite images.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, you said that your estimate was - and perhaps if one were to work on this carefully, it could be counted more precisely - there were about 20 bodies on that pile in the warehouse; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At that moment, I wasn't aware of the number. To this day, I think it's between 15 and 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, you say that you noticed a soldier. Did that soldier behave as if there was still gun-fire near him, or is he behaving as if there is no shooting around him, since you did hear gun-shots from the vicinity of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mean, the later viewing of this footage -- well, it's a bit contradictory the way he is walking around, and I remember that I heard gun-fire a lot along the road. Behind that hangar, as far as I can remember, there is a small river and that is the area where there were exchanges of gun-fire. I find it a bit strange now, but then I wasn't really paying any attention to it. It was too short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had there been shooting in the co-operative itself, do you believe that you would have seen that and that Borovcanin would have perhaps stopped to see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, had there been shooting, as different sources said, different witnesses said, well, perhaps I did not pass at that moment, but when I was passing, there was was shooting further away from the hangar, not in the hangar that was closed. But have you to know that I am just a witness of that moment, those three seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Borovcanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. As to whether you remember the door was closed or open, Dr. Petrovic, shall we upload the -- his transcript. Could you give the number, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P00375, Your Honour. It's the Popovic transcript, if that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And transcript page 18808. Through Mr. Nicholls, I asked you the question whether you remember seeing the bodies at the time in front of that warehouse. And you answered like this in the middle: "The witness: I didn't give it thought. Not this way. Yes, I saw it in two seconds. I had to register that as I was watching it through the camera's lens, but it was only two seconds long." My question is: In light of this, how do you remember whether the door was closed or open.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, as I said previously, I had my eye on the camera. As far as I can remember, that's two or three seconds. One, two, three. Not more than that. I had this image of the terrain where there was fighting. This I viewed later, when I was editing the programme. I probably recollect the editing moments better than the actual moments when I saw all of this, because, for example, I hadn't registered the presence of the soldier at all. It was really just a moment. And it's hard for me to say anything more than that. But it is evident that that is on my film. The door is closed, and the corpses are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So then Colonel Borovcanin went to see that soldier of his. Is it correct that the hands of the man had been burned because he had grabbed a barrel of a weapon that had been fired?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. President, as I was standing in front of the hospital, I did not go in with Borovcanin, I was told that he had injuries on his hands. I cannot remember exactly whether they had been cut up by a blade or whether there were burns on his hands. It was serious injury. Both would be serious injury, but perhaps it was that barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you to identify yet another interview of yours. 1D5636 could we have that called up. You mentioned in your testimony, Colonel Bunel. Is that a colonel of the French army that was part of the NATO force and that criticised the bombing of Serbia? Later on, he was also held accountable because he had warned the Serbs about the targets that would be hit.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Colonel Bunel, a military intelligence officer of the French army. He was even in prison because he provided information to the Serbs before the bombing. Before that, he served in Bosnia. I interviewed him twice. In the first interview, I didn't know that he had served in Bosnia. That was not our main topic. In the second interview, he told me astonishing things about the Muslims, that the Americans had taken into their base in Tuzla a few months later. That's what he said. So he should be asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he told you that a few months after the fall of Srebrenica, soldiers, Muslim soldiers, appeared from the woods, they appeared in the American base and that the American army transported them to the United States; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. For me, that was a shocking statement. However, no one seemed to care either in the Serbian public or in the international public. Later on, I found out, sometime in mid-1996 from people from the Serb diaspora - actually I wanted to shoot a documentary on that subject.
