I wanted to go to America to find these soldiers - Serbs signalled that a large group of people from Srebrenica had arrived in Virginia. But no one wanted to help me work on a documentary devoted to that topic, so that's the way it turned out. Is it shocking, as I said, that a colonel, a military intelligence man, would say something like, and, on the other hand, no one seemed to care. So these soldiers were hiding in the woods and were -- in these mountains, and they were grouped. And then a photographer from Tuzla actually took pictures of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have to admit that the relevance is not clear to me. This supposed transport in 1996 of somebody to America. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you explain the relevance, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, perhaps we can find them on the lists of missing persons and they're in Virginia or Salt Lake City. In America, thousands of Muslims are there; inter alia, some from Srebrenica. And the colonel saw them a few months after the fall of Srebrenica. He saw hundreds of soldiers who appeared from the woods in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will receive it as Exhibit D2254. And please continue. I note the time. It's about the time that you need to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I am just going to put a brief question before my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said that some other journalists viewed your material during the editing at Studio B and described them, is that unusual or impermissible; namely, that other journalists use material that was authored by someone else, another journalist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, could I have a cite, I may be wrong, to journalists viewing his material during the editing. He has talked about how people helped him with the editing which was done very quickly, because the -- it was broadcast immediately. I don't recall any testimony or statement that other journalists were present during the editing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness, today -- I think that the witness said today that he was angry because his copyright was abused because Robert Block viewed his material in an unauthorised way in the editing rooms of Studio B. If I'm wrong, then I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But could the witness kindly tell us whether that was the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said during the editing. Did Mr. Block see his video during the editing? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I mentioned Mr. Block, and only in 2012 I found out from the mentioned article written by Mr. Michael Dobbs, the great American journalist, who told me that Block had seen my materials. If that had been done to Christiane Amanpour or any other of the big names in journalism, he would have been wiped off. That is something that is not permissible at all. Without asking me, he was just rummaging through my material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you this: You knew this unit, and in your statements, you mentioned this special unit. And you said that we, as the government, were proud of them. Do you agree that we were proud of them because it was competent and because it abided by the rules and regulations and principles. On the other hand, tell me, are you aware of any misdeeds and misconduct on their part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I'm going to reiterate it once again, Mr. President, that in my view, and I was in many different situations in war, I think that this was a morally and militarily extremely and competent and excellent unit. There is not even a shadow of any crime committed by them in combat. If they hadn't had these characteristics, I wouldn't have been too keen to be in the same company with them. There is another motive why I looked for them. Christiane Amanpour prepared a report on the Black Swans and amongst them were even some of the Islamic fighters. She made a very pro-Muslim report. She was appraising the way they looked and how they were armed. Her report was a high-technical report because she had some ten people on her crew. I wanted to make a counter-report about our unit made up mainly of professional police officers. They were police officers even before the war, and this was an impeccable unit, and I can say that I am proud that I spent some time with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned today that Block made a big story of Kravica and that he even introduced the term genocide. Now, having known the entire leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, including myself, do you know whether any Serb official at any level had an inclination or was prepared to think and, let alone, do something towards destroying the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the people know me that I am merciless when it comes to the truth. I am now looking you in the eye, and I am telling you that I would be the first one that would destroy you in my articles had that been the case. I am not such a person, and I believe that the future will correct all the notions and misconceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were highly critical of President Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes. Particularly his wife, because she caused a lot of damage to our people. And you can see that proven in a scientific way from my book recently published in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, with this, I would like to finish my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Dr. Petrovic. First, this Colonel Bunel, Karadzic referred to him being punished. He was, in fact, convicted of treason; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That is true, Mr. Nicholls. But imagine treason and a conviction for that passed on someone who only two years later appears on television as a consultant. He spoke on the air about this, and you will admit that this is not a frequent occurrence had he really been a traitor. And it seems that all this was done on orders from some higher levels. I don't think that the French behaved so badly in the bombing of Serbia as the Americans and the others did. He only gave Serbs the information about the targets that were going to be hit. So this whole situation is rather odd. There's no precedent to the effect that a person convicted of treason later on appears on television and in other media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Going back to your comments about bin Laden being present in Bosnia and meeting with President Izetbegovic, I just want to make this clear. You learned this from a German journalist and the reason she gave you -- that nobody would publish it or take it seriously was that only a lunatic would believe it; is that right? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Just a slight correction. If he looked like a lunatic who was boasting about his grand motives, but he was dressed in a traditional way and this is how she explained it to me. However, knowing who she was and knowing her biography that she wrote for "Der Spiegel" which is a serious paper. I'm sure that that is her decision to write about it. But, obviously, the editor-in-chief didn't think that that was an interesting topic at the time, because the Germans took part in a large military procession in Bihac, together with Muslims. And she said that Mr. Werner would have been quite happy to see them there. And there are photographs which showed this. Now the point is that the policy was not to tackle this issue at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I now want to go back to -- there was some questioning today and you have testified about it before, basically the proposition that -- and you said it today, that Mr. Borovcanin wouldn't invite a journalist with him if there was a plan to murder people and commit crimes, and you said today and you said before that Mr. Borovcanin trusted you; right? He trusted you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would like to play a video-clip now from the 14th of July. This is from P00667 which is your raw footage, the -- that we copied from you. I will tell Mr. Reid. You should begin at 25:55.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. Can we stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We stopped at 26:07:1. I just want to make the point, if you recall, in the documentary, Studio B documentary, it's just after this scene that we see the short clip in front of Kravica warehouse; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep playing on the raw footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we could stop there, 26:55:09.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You have testified about this bit of footage before. My question is about this in relation to Mr. Borovcanin's trust of you. Now, here, you're calling Muslims, motherfuckers. You're laughing about the demolishment you see around you. You say: "Is this not your -- fuck, fuck their mothers, what have they brought us, a plague, motherfuckers." So did Mr. Borovcanin also think that Muslims were motherfuckers who brought a plague to Europe, to that -- your part of the country? Is that part of your bond with him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, this was a war situation, because you have to establish close bonds with those that you are with. You would have filmed the same thing whether you were on the Muslim side or the Croat side. I don't know why the vocabulary is so important, because this vocabulary is adapted to the situation. I met Mr. Borovcanin previously only twice and this was the third encounter, and we didn't talk much. I spoke more about what I saw what Hezbollah did in the Beqaa valley where they painted all the walls from the scenes of their history and Islam. So I am sitting in this car and this just came out as something -- that's what we are discussing while we were travelling from Bratunac to Srebrenica. I did say those things that I would have never said had the situation been normal, but I didn't attach any importance to this. I don't think that this would discredit me. I wanted to preserve the authenticity of the situation, and I think that it bears no relevance to this case at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. That helps me understand a bit better. You were speaking this way, if I understand you, you were adapting to the situation where you were with Mr. Borovcanin the day after the Kravica warehouse killings, that you were adapting yourself to being with Mr. Borovcanin? That's why you're talking about motherfuckers and a plague?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I would repeat that I had in mind the things had a been imported from the Middle East that had nothing to do with our European or Christian traditions, and I saw those things on the walls and I made comments. I didn't refer to all the Muslims as bastards. I never said that. I was only reliving my memories from Lebanon where I saw miles and miles of painted walls, and my reaction particularly referred to the Hezbollah, although this is not mentioned here. A director from Belgrade who used to be the husband of Natasa Kandic told me, We didn't want to cause any trouble for you for saying what you said. And he repeated the same thing that I heard today, which surprised me a lot. The whole story about him is a sad story. He, in addition to that, directed some of the footage that I made, and he signed my name as a cameraman. And he told me the same thing about six months ago in Belgrade, so I find it quite strange that you are repeating this today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Petrovic, I would like to have one thing clear: There was a portion of Mr. Nicholls' question that you didn't answer and can you possibly answer it for us, please. Did Borovcanin also think that the Muslims were motherfuckers? Can you answer that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the text in front of me on the screen. I don't know. When shall I start my answer? Your Excellency, as far as I can remember, Mr. Borovcanin, the then-Colonel and now General, never displayed any kind of intolerance towards Muslims. He used to be a school teacher, and I never heard him say anything bad about them, not only during this filming but during these two occasions when we briefly met. So he was not a person who would react in such a manner. I reacted here to the Beqaa valley because I had a feeling that I'm seeing a repetition of that in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But as for Ljubisa Borovcanin, he would never say such a thing in front of me. I don't remember him saying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one follow-up based on this Baqaa valley reference you're talking about, and I see how you say it's reminded you of a repetition in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You remember you were asked about this segment of the video in the Tolimir case. That's at T14456, and when you were asked about the -- this Arabic style, you said you were talking about some details on the walls of the houses that you saw referring, apparently, to Srebrenica. And you actually filmed some of those, is that right, that you were talking about what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Even in one piece of the footage when I'm talk to a former fighter who is coming back to his home and at some terrace on the first floor, I believe, the camera shows painting on the walls absolutely in the same style as the Hezbollah does in the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say Mr. Borovcanin would never say such things and agree that after you say, This is really demolished, fuck, this is already starting to look like some Arabic style. Mr. Borovcanin says, Yes, yes, yes. So did he agree with you or not about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nicholls, you ask me too much after so many years. I don't remember he got involved in that conversation at all. And I was really seeing it that way: The Middle East coming to our homes. It's like the Arabic Spring in Serb territory 20 years earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have P194, please. That's your article Mr. Karadzic showed you a little earlier. And one of the things you said, it's related to this same topic, is that nobody said anything bad. There was nothing unfriendly towards the Muslims. You didn't hear any abusive words, something that to effect today. Could we go -- this should be page 7 of the English -- 6 of the English - excuse me - which should be page 3 of the Serbian original. At the bottom of the page in English I will just quickly read it out: "Demographers will surely be interested in data that there were 10.000 children among the refugees. Out of that number, 8.000 were under the age of 3. The 'children of war,' as they call them. 'This is, you know, the concrete work of their hodzas. Fuck them. In total encirclement, with no food, constantly wailing but making kids at the same time. Is that normal? You cannot believe it. Now you tell me what kind of religion is that, Islam.'" And then on the next page in English, same page in the Serbian: "They have produced another corps in the centre of Srebrenica that will attack us again in 15 to 20 years. They had better stay out of our way. Fuck them. One could see that in a Potocari on the first sight each woman had a 'pack of kids hanging on her,' as Jevic put it." Okay, so this is a quote from Jevic, correct? These aren't your words. If you can explain.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [In English] Should I go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nicholls, I believe that this news report, as distinct from my television report where I did a poor job as a cameraman, is one of the best illustrations of that atmosphere. I don't think there's anybody here who should teach me how these news reports are written. I did it as everybody does it in the world. You come to a war zone, you want to document it. You record faithfully everything you hear. You are right. These are not my words, but they illustrate the atmosphere. I could also overhear the Muslims sitting on the bus where a Muslim woman was saying some interesting things. But let me just remind you, if you have a problem with this number of children, Mr. Vance from the Statement Department said that there were a total of around 40.000 people in Srebrenica, at least 10.000 under arms. And this is a fact that a demographer would find curious in that war situation. That is why my report remains a document forever. That was my job, not to iron out or wrap nicely whatever people said. I was a journalist there. What was going on was a conflict, a clash of two civilisations, the Christian and the Muslim one. And in the same situation I would again write the same report because my job was to document, to illustrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you answer the question now. This is it a quote from Dusko Jevic; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how the man introduced himself to me. I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and you know -- well, was he a subordinate of Borovcanin in the special police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I can answer only in terms of probability. If he was part of the special MUP unit, then he was, because Borovcanin was, at the time, the highest police officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at page 2 of the English, just to help you remember. Page 1 of the Serbian. You got his name bolded there, "Dusko Jevic and his specials were also giving out food," et cetera. Does that also help you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [In English] What was the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Does that help you remember that Dusko Jevic was a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now just tell me, that comment there about how the Muslims there are - I don't even know how to put it - breeding too much, having too many children, according to Dusko Jevic, and "They better stay out of our way. Fuck them." How does that fit with what you told Mr. Karadzic on cross-examination that there was no ill-will, no bad atmosphere? Can you explain it, ill will. I mean, is this friendly - I would just like you to explain - compassionate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That situation is a bit different, because that man in the field had been involved in the fighting for a week by then. All I saw on the faces of all the troops there is complete exhaustion. When you are exhausted you don't know what you are saying, because you can't raise that to the level of the level of the leadership of Republika Srpska, Mr. Karadzic and the other leaders. That's nonsense. I was just recording all that came out of the mouths of these people. It's important to know what kind of sentiment prevails because war is a dreadful thing. We all know that. People do and say all sorts of things. I did not want to do any self-censorship. If I had simply thrown out this passage, as I could have, we would not be having this conversation now. I was showing the sentiment on the Serbian side as well, and you see in a lot of my material that there are many things that are difficult to even hear for some American or European person who has never seen war. But my job was to make a report on a war that was still going on where the main fighting was over but there were many more battles ahead, and this man was well aware that there would be a lot more fighting because the Muslims had not surrendered yet. And Mr. Karadzic and others can confirm to you that heavy fighting was still going on. Little is known about that, and information is only now emerging. I was just trying to be very documentary in my approach. If I had known, I would show you some of my reports about Israel and Palestine, what the Palestinians and the Israelis say about each other and how they communicate. I know that this affects you, hits you very hard, you and the entire team, but I saw and heard this in a war, not on the streets of Paris. I was trying to depict the human side of the story, to record my first impressions unfiltered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said this, I think, if I understand about this article as well, what you just said. What you've got in this article is what you heard there, what you saw, not what you came up with yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: You see, 90 per cent of this text is actually quotation, except that I didn't put quotation marks everywhere. I -- throughout many of the sentences and turned into it a story, otherwise, it would have been a monologue, but all these things I heard from people in the streets, people I was with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Not to -- sorry, I was speaking too fast. I won't -- not -- to save time I won't bring it up, but there is a section in here called "bacon on the hot plate" or "slanina on the oven" or something, that talks about the need to get the scent of bacon into the walls so it stays forever. Just, what does that mean? You talked about pork and lamb, difference between peoples or something. What does that mean, getting pork into the walls so it stays forever?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: How can I drive it home to you? I tried already in the first part of my testimony when I talked to Mr. Karadzic. Let me give you an example. I come from a part of Serbia, I was born in Belgrade, first of all. But in the area where my parents come from, people eat mostly pork. My parents sometimes brought us roast lamb to Belgrade but my sister, my late sister, never wanted to eat that. That's not how we were raised. Those little episodes about lamb and pork, that concerned a place where a refugee had lived for three years, and it's a very different smell. Any Muslim from Bosnia will tell you they have the same antagonism towards pork. It's maybe a thing that is not very politically correct or very popular to say, but it's true. It's a clash of civilisations. One civilisation prefers pork, the other lamb. If you were a connoisseur or a sociologist, if you were very familiar with that region, you wouldn't need so much explanation. You would notice immediately. As soon as I go travel to Sarajevo I eat lamb. That's what I do. But this man was coming back to a house that used to be his and it suddenly smells of lamb. I was talking about realities. I was not making anything up. And it contributes to getting a better picture of what really happened in that war. It's a sociological picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay, let me look at one other part of the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me look at one other part of the article where you are talking about realities, not making anything up. It contributed to getting a better picture. It's page 3 of the English, Serbian page 2. Bottom of the page: "It seems that the first talks about the final elimination of the Srebrenica enclave and about the possibility to free quite a number of brigades tied in the enclave by the -- Oric's army have started at the beginning of the year. The Supreme Command of the RS, led by the president, Karadzic," in bold, "and with Mladic, Milovanovic, Gvero," et cetera, "along with a few other political figures of the 'so-called Republika Srpska' as foreign media but also some from Belgrade would put it, talked about Srebrenica on several occasions. In February, President Karadzic already had a clear vision on plans of the Main Staff of the VRS which guaranteed taking over Srebrenica." And then in the next paragraph you talk about Mladic getting the green light. Who did you learn that from while you were in Potocari and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably he needs to see the next paragraph in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where did you get that information from? Who told you about how these plans had begun and been exercised in the time-line, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot cite any names, but a number of these officers who were in the field then, including Borovcanin, told me a few things. But I picked up here and there these things, and that article appeared on the 21st of July. When I finished editing my video material I had more time to dedicate to this, to make a chronology of events for myself. Of course, I was not at Pale. I was not able to find all that out. And there is even an error here as to who was part of these units. I had a wrong piece of information. General Gvero was not part of that group. And I cannot tell you the names of all my sources, but these are normal sources for journalists that provide a complete picture, because not a single military operation can be planned within three days. This is a very hastily produced article published in end July. If I had written it in 2006, it would have been different. I may have gotten a few details wrong, but I cannot give you the names. The sources were in the military, of course, but also analysts, analysts from Belgrade and elsewhere. There were many people who followed these events, the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me move on. You talked and it's your interview with me from 2006, I think - we saw at e-court pages 115 and 116 - about how apparently the Bosnian Serb leadership saw the Studio B documentary, asked for a copy, got sent up by bus, and then the feedback you got was that they thought it was very positive and balanced and a good thing. And you said in the interview that Krajisnik, you knew, saw it. So my question is: Try to remember now who was it? Do you have any details you didn't remember before? Do you remember now how you got the message from the Bosnian Serb leadership, if I call it that, that they approved of your video documentary? If you don't remember, that's all right. But I just wonder if you remember now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I am willing to assist. Please make no mistake. I'm thinking. Studio B is a city television. They could not see it at Pale at the time. So it must have been somebody from Republika Srpska in Belgrade who saw it and told the people at Pale. I don't remember, although I had interviewed Mr. Krajisnik before, as well as all the other leaders, expect Mladic. He was the only one to whom I never gained access. They said that probably through journalists who -- their own journalists or foreign journalists who are based in Belgrade. They were close to the leadership and they could get interviews from them, and I suppose they told me. One of the journalists told me. But it -- I know that it's not they who told me directly. And we sent the tape to them by bus. Zoran Zaharijevic [phoen] was involved in that. But they were certainly unable to see that footage until we sent them the tape. They couldn't see it on satellite TV, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did anyone from the Bosnian Serb leadership come down to you and say, Hey, we saw your documentary. There's a pile of bodies in front of a warehouse. Can you tell us more about that? Where is this? What's going on? We're concerned about this pile of corpses in your documentary.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I can't remember, Mr. Nicholls. I would have remembered if it had been Mr. Krajisnik, especially Mr. Karadzic, from whom I had not heard for long at the time [as interpreted]. None of them contacted me directly. It must have been through our common journalist contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That they let me know their reaction through those journalists. Or perhaps they even called Studio B. I can't know that. I was not full-time employed with Studio B. I was just one of their correspondents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know Dragan Cicic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: I know who that is. He was a journalist for the "Nin" magazine, a leading Serbian weekly. He was not a career journalist. He turned up out of nowhere and started writing for the "Nin" magazine. I never actually talked to the man. We just exchanged hellos around the office when I passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You made some pretty serious allegations against Robert Block, calling him a liar, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [In English] Block.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Block, yeah.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Excuse me, [Interpretation] Cicic called him a liar or I? I did call him a liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You called Robert Block a liar in court today. That's what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now I'm just going to put it to you: Did you speak with Mr. Block and Dragan Cicic after the Studio B documentary had been aired, after Mr. Block published his article, "Bodies pile up in horror of Srebrenica" in "The Independent," which referred to your article, and expressed that you were angry at him, that he had no right to have used your tape and that it had gotten you in trouble with the authorities in the RS which is completely contrary to what you say about them being pleased with the content?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Excuse me, for laughing. I would have to have complete amnesia regarding my entire life to accept this. What's funny is that Cicic is turning up in this story because Block was accompanied by Grubacic all the time. That's the first oddity in what you are saying. He was the first one who reviewed my material after reading Michael Dobbs, the article I mentioned in the foreign policy magazine. I don't remember talking to him. If it were just a hello, I could have forgotten, but if I had spoken to him at length -- and can you really imagine that I would tell a foreign journalist that Karadzic and his team were angry with me? I still claim that it's a complete fabrication. I have no reason to claim that he hadn't been with me if he had. I didn't even have to mention the contact I had with him in Bratunac. But I remember absolutely nothing about seeing him in Belgrade, and that's why I call him a liar, because as soon as somebody gets into somebody's place and takes something that doesn't belong to him he both a thief and a liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, one, you're absolutely sure you remember seeing Robert Block in Belgrade. And I ask you that because his testimony is that -- I mean, excuse me, in Bratunac, when you were there. Because his testimony, I have to be fair, put it to you, in this case, and it has been consistent, was that he never crossed the Drina river into the Republika Srpska, that his reporting was done on the Serbian side of Ljubovija bridge. He was not able to get to Bratunac, even though he tried. So think carefully. Did you see him in Bratunac, or are you making a mistake?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: He was absolutely in Bratunac, but he hadn't crossed the Drina to arrive in Bratunac like I did. He had been there a while, and Braca Grubacic will confirm, if he is honest. They had come from the territory of Republika Srpska, not from Serbia. That's the first thing that he is saying that is untrue. That's what he said to me. We have been travelling around Bosnia for a while, and we are coming now here to see what's going on. That's what he told me. And he was accompanied by somebody who served as his interpreter at the same time and he was collecting stories. First of all, Block was never called here before I mentioned him, and his articles started appearing already on the 16th and 17th July. And they were a serious landmark for all the other journalists reporting on Srebrenica, that 500, 600 people were killed in a school house in Bratunac. A normal person could not invented something like that, could not write something like that. Perhaps he did not say 1500 but he said hundreds. I saw him in Bratunac. Somebody introduced him, and even Ljubisa Borovcanin also said hello to him. I can't remember who accompanied him, but there were four of us standing in the streets of -- in Bratunac. Why would Bratislav Grubacic be there in that year? He had a magazine called "VIP," and he was a very well respected source from Serbia for foreign journalists, and he had a lot of political experience, but he was there just as an escort, a journalist escort, to that foreign journalist. Why would I have made up Block's presence there, because I was surprised to see him there as an Englishman. And let me add one thing. He could have been there only thanks to his connections with the regime in Belgrade. Somebody must have intervened with the army to let him through. That was the only way he was able to walk freely around there without any escort. He was not under surveillance. He was only with Grubacic, nobody from the army. Nobody was watching him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You remember him as being an English journalist?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Well, we say English. It can also be an American who worked for the English. To this day, I don't know whether is he an American. But usually people say English. Maybe he was an American who worked for "The Independent"; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you one question before I think we're -- we're at the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have more?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A little bit, Your Honour, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will take a break for an hour and resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest that we take a shorter break, because I would just like to ask for ten minutes and then we could finish early today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Those representations in the past by Mr. Karadzic about how long he's going to take have not been accurate. And we haven't ever had ended up finishing early when we said we would. I just have to make that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Doctor Pirocanac, I'm going to -- Dr. Petrovic, excuse me --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will try to finish off very quickly now. All right. Still on the topic of Mr. Block's statement. He didn't publish it in any articles but his statement that you told him that President Karadzic himself was angry over the footage, speaking of the Studio B footage. You're laughing.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll ask you the question now. Could I have 1D5116, please. This is a Defence document, Mr. Petrovic, Dr. Petrovic. I will let you it was used when Mr. Block testifies [sic] here. This is an e-mail from Dragan Cicic to Mr. Robinson, the attorney working with Mr. Karadzic, and very quickly, Mr. Robinson asked the question, if you see on the seconds paragraph on the bottom pardon: "An issue has come up in Mr. Karadzic's trial relating to your visit with Robert Block to Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac at his apartment after you reviewed the Studio B footage." And the answer, I'm trying to save time, if you look up, Dragan Cicic writes: "I do remember that Mr. Petrovic-Pirocanac said that he got in trouble with the authorities of Republika Srpska because of his footage. "I do not recall whether he specifically mentioned Dr. Karadzic by name, though did I assume at the time that his reference is included all the people in the leadership of Republika Srpska." So, again, does that jog your memory of meeting not just with Mr. Block but also with Dragan Cicic in your apartment in Belgrade after the tape disappeared from Studio B, and you saying that you got in -- -- that the Republika Srpska leadership was angry? Or can you explain why Dragan Cicic says this, if it didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: First of all, I live in no apartment. I live in a house that is 22 kilometres away from Belgrade. I don't know if you asked about the address of this "apartment" of mine. That is a small detail that would be of interest to you as an investigator. Secondly, I remember another man very well, whom you've never called in. He is quite interesting. He was sitting with me in Studio B. His last name is Schiller. He's from the "Toronto Star" or some other Canadian daily. He sat with me at the editing room. He was with Naser Oric in Srebrenica. He said to me, and he said that he saw Serb heads rolling, as they were cut off. He sat there and watched me edit this TV programme, Schiller, and he looks like that American actor who is a comedian and who has grey hair. I can't remember his name now. But anyway, I remember, Schiller, and I assume I'd remember Block, too. I repeat to you once again, Block. I mean, that looks to me like the story about that Dutch journalist who came to see me at home. He provoked me, and at one moment I said, Well, I don't even want to talk about it anymore. He maltreated me with this raw material. This is before you got the original of my TV programme. So it is only in that context that Block falls into the picture. I mean, if you were to call me people at home while I'm sitting here and ask, Was he ever at our home? I mean, I tell you, I can guarantee that Cicic never came to see me. He said apartment. And I live in no apartment. I live in a big house in a village. So this is not a reliable witness, and this angers me. Sorry about that. But why would this Mr. Nobody, Cicic, and Block invent all of this? I was honest with you. I told you the truth. And Block is in the story about Bratunac. Didn't he publish his story about rumours in Bratunac already on the 16th and 17th; namely, that hundreds of people were killed in the school. That is what they came up with, on the basis of rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Dr. Petrovic. Can I remind you that it is not Mr. Cicic that referred to your apartment. It is Mr. Robinson that referred to your apartment and all that Mr. Cicic said in this alleged e-mail correspondence is that he remembered that you said that you got in trouble with the authorities of Republika Srpska because of your footage. That's all that he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Excellency, I will clarify. [Interpretation] So, in this letter, Cicic says that I got into trouble with the authorities of Republika Srpska. He is no friend of mine. I never socialised with the man. I would not be confessing to him that Republika Srpska held certain things against me. The truth is quite different, but that has nothing to do with Cicic's inventions. I had trouble with different soldiers from Republika Srpska, and I received threats to the effect that I would be killed because of your report, the one that you see here. But this really has nothing to do with the authorities of Republika Srpska. Indeed, if that were the case, I wouldn't be testifying here now with Mr. Karadzic. Sorry for saying this. This is staged, as the Americans would say, and it's a completely foolish thing. There is no reason for me not to remember him. [In English] "I do not recall whether he specifically mentioned Dr. Karadzic by name, though I did assume at the time that his reference included all the people in the leadership of Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] Your Excellency, once again, I repeat, this is an absolutely. Several times I had this opportunity. I mean, people from French television know about that. I received threats. But these are individuals from Republika Srpska who were not pleased when they saw my report. But the anti-war lobby in Belgrade was not pleased with it either; that is to say that they were both against it. But this really has nothing to do with the leadership of Republika Srpska. Not in any way, not in any point in time. Let me repeat once again. I found out about this only late. I think that I mentioned that at General Tolimir's trial twice. Prominent -- no, they're not prominent. At one point in time, General Mladic prevented someone from killing me. That's what journalists told me. That's one thing. And the other time was that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, heard that some of his people were talking about that, about this idea of killing me, and he prevented that. And that is why I appear before you today, because I had not been assassinated but this had nothing to do with the leadership of Republika Srpska. I was on excellent terms with them, especially with President Karadzic and madam vice-president, Biljana Plavsic, until she became president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because I think you have answered the question. I have very little time. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask a further question, Mr. Nicholls. You just stated, Dr. Petrovic, that you had trouble with different soldiers from Republika Srpska. Can you be more specific about that? Who threatened you or for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, Your Excellencies, I never encountered the people who did that, but I did receive threats from different quarters, journalists included. I remember when one of my woman colleagues when she crossed over to Republika Srpska was asked by some soldiers, Where is that Pirocanac? We're waiting for him. She can confirm that any time, if anyone asks her in Belgrade. Also, there were other sources that I consider to be a warning so that I would be aware what was going on. I established that this had nothing to do with the political levels of Republika Srpska, but many were dissatisfied with my report and it turned out that it was a very important source to find out more about these events. I don't know what the point is of this renowned journalist, quote/unquote, Dragan Cicic to say all of this, or perhaps I've just deleted all this from my memory. But how would that be possible? How is it that I remember Schiller from Canada who was with me during those days precisely? Had Blocked asked me, he could have seen this while sitting next to me. The "Bowl of Stones" is the name of a book that was written by a man who was in Belgrade, and he was there for a month and he saw a lot of people there and then he mocked me and other people later on. He ridiculed us. He watched the material when I was editing it. You can check this. Two men watched the material as I was editing it, so why would I not agree to this third one? I wasn't aware of this until recently, until Michael Dobbs wrote about this, and I trust Michael Dobbs more than I trust this Block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It -- in relation to Mr. Cicic's comment that you got in trouble with the authorities of Republika Srpska, can one not view military leaders as part of authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, of course. But that had nothing to do with Mladic or with any other senior officers. You have to know that my criticism of Republika Srpska was because it was not all right and proper. It is not that all soldiers on the front line were at war. There were parts that were under poor military control, which, in part, explains what happened in Srebrenica, as revenge, which is impermissible in the military. But there are no leaders involved. I absolutely claim that that is an invention. Even if he had seen me, as he did not, I mean, I only saw the man at the "Nin" office and much later at that. So, in this situation, I did not see him with this Block, and I think that this is a miserable fabrication. I have no reason not to mention them. They are of no significance for Srebrenica at all. They are a small fry, or peanuts, if you will. But I still don't see what the point is of this, and I completely deny their allegations. If you want, we can take a lie detector test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after the, as you say, authorities of Republika Srpska requested a copy of the tape, and after it disappeared in unknown ways from Studio B, when we received a copy of your raw data, some of the missing parts were scenes of the bodies in front of the Kravica warehouse and the men on the balcony replaced by the shell casings, among other parts, missing [sic]. You've never - and correct me if I'm wrong - been able to explain how it is that coincidentally those are the parts missing from the documentary -- from the documentary that are missing on your raw footage; is that right? You still can't explain that. [Microphone not activated] Is it a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I don't think that your last word was translated because microphone was not activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] My question was: Is it a coincidence. I had the wrong -- is it a coincident, was the last part.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Nicholls, here we come again. [Interpretation] For the umpteenth time I'm going to say this now. I'm still astonished by the fact that practically never they used the actual material of the programme but only the raw material, which is unfair, in my view. So if my 8-millimetre cassette, which is not professional, this is an amateur tape, if it is given to, I don't know how many addresses, over a certain period of time, whoever asked me to view this was given opportunity to do so, many journalists from throughout the world who were in our part of the world. We can only assume now what happened. But it's not only that those scenes were deleted that appear in the original, others were as well. You did not mention that at one point in time there is a studio where Radovan Karadzic was, and I was with the Frenchman a year before that, I went to see him, I mean. I already told you I'm not a cameraman. I had that as well, so then there were traces of that as if you will. Then Mr. Blasik saw this in my home, these empty tank shells on my terrace. You will agree with me that it is impossible for me not -- I mean, this situation cannot be resolved. Obviously we are never going to find out what happened, and I'm saying that for the benefit of the public and my own country as well, as I have told you so many times. You have the originals. The Court has the originals, and for years they were considered to be missing pictures, erased pictures. So that exists there and I think that that is what matters the most, for history and for your work. And I assume that someone should say thank you to me at some point for all this. But, no, in Belgrade, to this day, there are manipulations that are bandied about in 2012. Do tell the entire public of the former Yugoslavia once and for all that this footage exists, that you have it. The people on the terrace of the white house and those three seconds by the hanger as we are passing by, I think that this is a huge contribution of mine as a journalist. I wish it could have been even greater, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I believe that the learned Mr. Nicholls brought in a great deal or new material, so I kindly ask for additional time to put additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us which is new and what kind of questions you are going to put to the witness. Just first tell us which part of Mr. Nicholls' re-examination introduced new factors.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hodzas and birth-rate. That is one important thing. Then there are other things as well but this is the most important. And also, the presence of Islam from the Middle East and clashes within the Muslim society itself on account of that. A few brief matters. And I will kindly ask the witness to give yes or no answers and it's not going to be long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear from you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to use any of my time, Your Honours, but I don't believe anything -- that I opened any new doors. I used the article which Mr. Karadzic used, and I don't think I opened any doors and it's not warranted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just respond. In an effort to impeach the credibility of this witness, the Prosecution put to him slurs, essentially, that were made on the tape concerning the Muslims, and those were not something that arose during the cross-examination. It was proper to do that on [indiscernible] examination. But, in any event, those are subjects that Dr. Karadzic wishes to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where that arose, Your Honour, was the proposition put by Mr. Karadzic to the witness that he was allowed to film anything. There was no censorship placed on him by Mr. Borovcanin and that there were no controls, to try to show that there would be no plan and that nothing -- no crimes were planned or committed. My point was to show, as Mr. Petrovic-Pirocanac said before, he was trusted. He was trusted to do the right thing by Mr. Borovcanin, and indeed -- I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that Mr. Nicholls' cross-examination is absolutely legitimate and there's nothing new that warrants further questions by the Defence. However, given the situation, we'll give you the leave to ask one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Petrovic, I quoted only part of that text here, but the other parts seem to indicate that soldiers said that the number of children is the result of the work of hodzas. Do you remember that the "Reis-Ulema," the supreme leader of the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mustafa Ceric, on the 17th of July, 1994, issued a public "fatwa" that -- mainly that every Muslim woman should bear at least five children. It became public then, but it was probably in effect considerably before that. Do you link this to what this man said, that the number of children is the result of the work of the hodzas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure your microphone is activated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Excellency. [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is not only I, but many journalists and analysts from the former Yugoslavia, know of this statement. He represents the more militant part in Bosnia. He will be replaced soon. But you put it well. There are Muslims in Bosnia who are not of this dangerous ilk. They are people who respect their faith, but do not do what Ceric does, not like what the Muslim leader in Serbia is doing, running for president which is unheard of on this planet. Professor Ivo Kosta [phoen], my professor from Paris, one of the greatest geographers, demographers and geo-politologist from the -- all over the world, he will tell you that this principle was applied in our part of the world for decades, and reaching these numerical levels was only done for these geo-strategic reasons. And also Colonel Bunel published a few books and refers to that in some of his books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC-PIROCANAC
utterances.text: If you allow me just one more sentence, and I think it would be useful for their Excellencies and for Mr. Nicholls and everyone else. When one says "plan," this absence of a plan, in the awareness of the Serbs and most of the other ethnic communities in our part of the world, is the gravest problem of all. The only successful planned thing that was done over the past 50 or 60 years was the success of Djokovic. However, individually or collectively, there is no situation when we succeeded in planning something and accomplishing something, nothing else. We never carry things through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, if you agree that many Serbs, including myself, consider Muslims to be Serbs, and that all great people who were Muslims were Serbs as well, do you agree that at this point in time within the Muslim society there is a situation whereby some Muslims are firmly opposed to the import of Middle Eastern Islam that the Bosnian Muslims are not used to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any relevance. No. We'll --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain, Your Excellencies? Just a few words why that is important. It is important because Dr. Petrovic documented certain statements that paint a picture of a certain moment in time, and that those were negative statements made by the Serbs against the Muslims. But which Muslims did they have in mind? If we consider the Muslims to be the Serbs, we should clarify what their target was and which particular aspect of Islam is being targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber does not see any relevance to this case. Then that concludes your evidence, Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Excellency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just a second. To be fair, since we gave leave to the accused to put his last question, if you have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you want to say something, Dr. Petrovic? No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I need some assistance, if possible. It is not very well known in the public, and I would like Mr. Karadzic to confirm this, it so happens that I was supposed to become his Chief of Staff at the beginning of the war, but I had to reject his offer because I was afraid that somebody from Belgrade was going to assassinate me. We know that Mr. Milosevic's wife was a staunch Stalinist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, Dr. Petrovic, the Chamber does not usually entertain further comments from the witness. We'll stop here. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for coming to The Hague yet again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you are free to go. Unless there are any other matters to be raised, we will rise all together. Then we will resume tomorrow at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 4th day of May, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.03 p.m.,
